headline: You can flatten a few small pads with little paperwork if all digging and clearing stays more than 50 ft from every Joshua tree, and earthwork stays at 100 cubic yards or less in the county. Map every tree on and near the lot before you make an offer.
key_points: You can build, grade and clear anywhere more than 50 ft from every western Joshua tree without a state tree permit. Within 50 ft, any land disturbance needs approval from the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) first. That covers the house, the trailer pad, pods, septic, trenches, fences, solar, sheds, containers, driveways, grading and brush clearing. Trees on a neighbor's lot within 50 ft of your work count too.

You can do the Joshua tree census yourselves. CDFW lists the property owner as an acceptable preparer. The census covers the work area plus a 15 m (about 50 ft) buffer. Every stem that rises from the ground counts as its own tree. A hand-drawn map is fine for projects with fewer than 10 trees. Ask neighbors' permission where the buffer crosses their land.

You can apply to remove a tree with an Incidental Take Permit (ITP), but it is slow and costly. The whole Morongo Basin, including Yucca Valley, is in CDFW's standard fee area. The 2026 in-lieu fees per stem are $354.75 under 1 m (about 3 ft), $521.75 for 1-5 m (about 3-16 ft) and $2,609 for 5 m (about 16 ft) or taller. You pay the rate in effect on the day you pay. CDFW must re-set fees by June 30, 2027.

An ITP needs a tree census, site plans and California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) paperwork, and the timing has no fixed end (ask CDFW Region 6 for current processing times). CDFW issued only 41 ITPs statewide from July 2024 to June 2025, and 29 of them were in San Bernardino County. Designing around the trees is cheaper and faster. CDFW Region 6 issues every Joshua tree permit, both inside the Town of Yucca Valley and in the unincorporated county: r6cesa@wildlife.ca.gov, (909) 484-0167.

Free CDFW Hazard Management Permits cover dead trees. They also cover trimming live trees that have fallen within 30 ft of a structure, lean on one, or pose an imminent threat. They never allow removing a living tree. Assembly Bill (AB) 1808 (September 2026) lets owner-occupants of an existing house remove up to 10 trees near it. So it does not help with the first house on vacant land. CDFW has not posted its forms yet (ask CDFW Region 6).

You can clear most desert plants after getting a county Tree or Plant Removal Permit. It covers all yuccas (including Mojave yucca), agaves and nolinas, creosote rings 10 ft or wider, smoke trees and mesquite with stems 2 in or thicker or 6 ft or taller, and any part of an ironwood, mesquite or palo verde. Removal within 20 ft of a structure built under a county permit is exempt from the county permit only, never from the state Joshua tree law. These rules come from the 2007 Development Code as compiled in 2014. Ask San Bernardino County Land Use Services (LUS) about later changes, and ask Town Planning if the lot is in the Town.

You can move up to 100 cubic yards of cut plus fill without a county grading permit. The building official can still require one in sensitive areas. Hillside standards apply at a natural slope of 15% or more. You need no soils engineer if the slope is 20% or less and the lot is outside fault, landslide and liquefaction zones. In the Town, hillside review applies at 15% or steeper once grading exceeds 500 cubic yards per lot or disturbance exceeds 10,000 sq ft (ask Town Planning).

You can keep a grading permit simple. Keep cut and fill slopes at 2:1 or flatter, and keep retaining walls at 4 ft or lower. Walls over 4 ft (footing bottom to wall top) need their own permit. Fees are roughly $693-$775 for 100-1,000 cubic yards, plus plan review, and about $369 for an erosion and sediment control permit (estimate; ask County LUS at (909) 387-8311). A grading plan review expires 180 days after filing.

A gentle slope means little earthwork. Take a 50 x 40 ft pad on an 8% slope, with its long side along the contour. It needs about 30 cubic yards of cut and 30 of fill, and the deepest cut is about 1.6 ft. Turning the long side downhill adds about 25%. A driveway, pods and 24 in of over-excavation under footings can push the total past 100 cubic yards. Pods on piers or screw piles need almost no grading.

You can clear what you need, but not the whole lot. Keep total disturbed ground under 1 acre (43,560 sq ft) to avoid the state stormwater Construction General Permit. On desert lots of 1 acre or more, the county allows clearing only for pads, driveways, landscaping and agriculture. Fire access sets the driveway's shape. It must be at least 12 ft wide and no steeper than 12% (gravel or native surface only up to 8%), with a turnaround if it is longer than 150 ft.

You can build on high ground between washes. Changing even a dry wash needs a Lake or Streambed Alteration (LSA) notification to CDFW, filed through the Environmental Permit Information Management System (EPIMS). CDFW decides within 30 days whether the notification is complete. If no draft agreement arrives within 60 days after that, you may go ahead as described. Keep septic 50 ft from any drainage course. Never send extra runoff onto neighbors.

You can start clearing once a biologist has surveyed the site. The Mojave desert tortoise has been state-endangered since July 15, 2025. The western burrowing owl (since October 2024) and Bendire's and LeConte's thrashers (since April 2026) are state candidates, which get the same protection as listed species.

risks.risk: Grading, clearing, or setting a trailer, pod or septic within 50 ft of a Joshua tree without CDFW approval counts as illegal take. CDFW can prosecute, and the county can hold up your permits.
risks.mitigation: Count and map the trees before buying. Flag or fence every 50-ft buffer before any machine arrives. Get CDFW's answer in writing for any work near a buffer. Never tidy brush around the trees.

risks.risk: The lot has no tree-free building area. That means fees of $354.75-$2,609 per stem, CEQA paperwork, consultant costs and no fixed timeline.
risks.mitigation: Make the purchase depend on a census that shows clear pad sites. Renegotiate or walk away if there are none.

risks.risk: Pads, the trailer or stored belongings sit in or below a wash, and a flash flood damages them while you are in Bhutan.
risks.mitigation: Check the federal and state flood maps and look for signs of a wash on the lot. Build on high ground, with swales uphill to divert water and rock at their outlets. Leave washes untouched.

risks.risk: As pads, the driveway, septic, orchard prep and staging add up, disturbed ground passes 1 acre or earthwork passes 100 cubic yards. That triggers a state stormwater permit or a county grading permit, with engineered plans.
risks.mitigation: Keep a running tally of square feet disturbed and cubic yards moved. Put pods on piers, keep the driveway narrow, and dig orchard basins by hand.

risks.risk: A tortoise, an owl burrow or a thrasher nest turns up mid-project. Work stops until CDFW is consulted.
risks.mitigation: Have a biologist check the site within a few days before clearing. Clear in fall or early winter, outside nesting season. Keep a written plan: stop work and call CDFW.

risks.risk: Bare graded soil blows away and erodes, or a permit or grading plan review lapses while you are away. Plan reviews expire 180 days after filing.
risks.mitigation: Do not start grading you cannot finish before a trip. Gravel and stabilize every pad. Pass an inspection right before you leave.

questions_for_couple: If your favorite house spot has a Joshua tree within 50 ft, will you move the house, pay $354.75-$2,609 per stem and wait an unknown time for a permit, or walk away from the lot?
What is the smallest footprint for day one (house pad, trailer pad, driveway, septic), and what can wait until after the final inspection?
Will you put pods on piers or screw piles so you barely grade, even if they cost more up front?
Will you count and flag the trees yourselves, or pay a consultant up to about $3,000 (estimate)?
How much will you spend on site work before the house itself (survey, biologist, engineer, grading)? Roughly $8,000-$30,000 is a realistic range (estimate).
Will you dig orchard basins by hand and keep the driveway narrow to stay under 1 acre of disturbance, or budget $3,000-$12,000 for a state stormwater permit instead (estimate)?
Where should the orchard and native plants go so they catch runoff from the roof and pads while staying out of the 50-ft tree buffers?
next_actions: Look up the parcel's Assessor's Parcel Number (APN) on the San Bernardino County parcel map viewer. Note whether it is inside the Town of Yucca Valley or in the unincorporated county, and note its zoning (for example RL-5). (@computer)

Check the lot on three maps: the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Flood Map Service Center (msc.fema.gov), the Department of Water Resources Best Available Maps (gis.bam.water.ca.gov/bam), and the California Geological Survey EQ Zapp fault and landslide map. Screenshot each result. (@computer)

Spend one morning on the lot during the November-December 2026 visits with a phone GPS app. Flag, photograph and size every Joshua tree stem, including small ones under shrubs and any within 50 ft past the lot lines. Use the columns from CDFW's census instructions as your field sheet. (@land)

Load the tree points into Google Earth and draw a 50-ft circle around each one. Sketch where the house pad, trailer pad, septic and leach field, driveway and 1-2 pods fit outside the circles and outside washes. Draw an elevation profile across each possible pad and mark whether its slope is under 15% and under 20%. (@computer)

Email CDFW Region 6 at r6cesa@wildlife.ca.gov with the APN, tree map and sketch. Ask whether a plan kept more than 50 ft from all trees needs any CDFW sign-off, how long ITPs currently take, and when AB 1808 forms will be posted. (@email)

Call San Bernardino County Land Use Services at (909) 387-8311. Ask about current grading and erosion-control permit fees, and whether the 100-cubic-yard limit counts all phases together. Also ask whether the desert native plant rules have changed since 2014, and whether the parcel is in a sensitive area that needs a grading permit anyway. (@phone)
If the lot is inside the Town, call Town of Yucca Valley Community Development (Planning). Ask for its grading limits, native-plant rules and Joshua tree steps in writing. (@phone)

Request quotes from 2 licensed land surveyors (boundary corners plus 1-ft contours of the building area). Also request one from a desert biologist (a check of your tree census plus a tortoise, owl and nesting-bird survey in one visit). (@email)
Talk with the downhill and next-door neighbors. Ask where storm water runs and whether you may count their trees within 50 ft of the shared line. (@land)

Write a due-diligence contingency for the January-February 2027 offer. It should cover the tree census, flood zone, fault zone and septic feasibility within the 45-60 day due-diligence period. (@together)
